scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user is a high school senior who's been staying home due to school closures. She has a younger sister, and their mom expects them to cook dinner every night because they're home all day. The user is upset because she has schoolwork to do and feels that her mom isn't contributing, especially since the mom is a bad cook and doesn't help out. The user refused to cook one night, leading to an argument with her mom. The dad usually cooks because the mom doesn't, and he's the one who ended up cooking that night.

First, I need to understand the dynamics here. The mom expects the kids to cook every night, but she herself doesn't contribute much. The dad is the primary cook and does most of the chores. The user feels burdened by the expectation to cook while managing schoolwork. She's also frustrated that her mom doesn't help despite having the time.

I should consider the roles and responsibilities within the family. Typically, parents are expected to handle the household responsibilities, especially when they're the ones with jobs outside the home. The user and her sister are still students, so their primary focus should be on their education. The mom's expectation that they cook every night might be unreasonable, especially if she isn't contributing herself.

The user's refusal to cook could be seen as a form of protest against the unfair distribution of responsibilities. She's asserting her need to focus on schoolwork, which is a valid concern. However, refusing to help entirely might not be the best approach. It could lead to tension and make the situation worse.

On the other hand, the mom's behavior seems problematic. She's not taking responsibility for her own role in the household and is placing undue pressure on her children. It's unfair to expect teenagers to manage all the cooking while they're dealing with their own academic responsibilities.

The dad's role is interesting. He's taking on most of the household duties, which might be contributing to the tension. If he's the one who usually cooks, maybe the mom feels less inclined to help. It might be a systemic issue within the family that needs addressing.

In terms of morality, the user's action of refusing to cook could be seen as self-advocacy. She's standing up for her own needs, which is important. However, the way she handled it might not be the most constructive. It led to an argument, which isn't ideal. Maybe there's a better way to communicate her feelings without refusing to help entirely.

The mom's reaction was also extreme. Getting angry and calling the kids useless isn't appropriate. It's important for parents to model respectful communication and take responsibility for their own actions.

Overall, while the user's refusal to cook might not be the best approach, her underlying reasons are valid. The situation highlights a need for better communication and a more equitable distribution of responsibilities within the family.
